en: The Thirteen-Book Collection of Birth Stories (Jātaka),
Chapter on Mangoes (Ambavagga)
8. The Takkāriya Jātaka “I alone am the fool who spoke ill,
calling the excellent bear ‘snake’ in the Himālaya forest.”
“Takkāriya, I am falling into this pit;
it is surely not good to speak excessively.
“The mortal who speaks excessively meets with ruin.”
"Regarding bondage, execution, sorrow, and lamentation,
you alone should blame yourself in this matter,
O teacher, for they are burying you in a pit."
"Why did I ask Tuṇḍila whether he would provide his brother with a meal on the Kāḷikā day?
Why did I let him go naked, deprived of his pair of garments?"
“This matter is also just like the case of the many.
“The quail that, while they were fighting, did not fight,
but flew up into the space between the rams;”
Thus they were crushed there by the heads of the rams;
this matter is much like the previous one.
Four men seized the book.
While protecting even a single person,
they all lay down with their heads shattered;
this matter, too, is much like the former one.
Just as a goat tied in a bamboo thicket,
while trying to escape, fell right into the midst of a sword;
by that very [sword], its throat was cut.
“This matter, too, is much like that.
“These are neither gods nor sons of gandhabbas;
these are deer who have come to me for the sake of their own welfare.”
"Let them cook one for the evening meal,
and let them cook one again for the morning meal.
"A hundred thousand ill-spoken words..."
They do not equal even a fraction of well-spoken words;
ill-spoken speech is a defilement that leads one astray.
Therefore, O Kimpurisas, you should remain silent and not act like fools.
“Let her who has spoken thus be released;
let them lead her to Mount Himavat;
and let them give this one to the kitchen.”
“Let them cook it for him at the morning meal early in the day.
“Cattle have the rain as their lord;
this people has cattle as its lord.”
"You are the lord, O Great King;
I am the lord of my wife.
Having recognized one of these two,"
Once freed, one might go to the mountain.
Indeed, blame cannot be entirely avoided;
O Lord of Men, various kinds of people must be encountered.
By the very same means by which one gains praise,
another gains a critic.
The entire world is full of attachment and full of aversion.
The entire world is possessed of mind within the mind;
all beings are distinct with their individual minds.
Who here can act according to the power of another's mind?
“The Kimpurisa remained silent along with his wife,
who had now spoken out because he was afraid of danger;
now he is released, happy, and free from illness.”
"Speech makes men wealthy.
Thus ends the eighth Jātaka, the Takkāriya Jātaka.
